messages.content:
Fix \(p\in(1,2)\cup(2,\infty)\) and put \(q=p/(p-1)\). A matrix weight is a measurable function \(W:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C^{2\times2}\) whose entries are locally integrable and whose values are Hermitian positive definite almost everywhere. Matrix powers are defined by spectral calculus. Write \(|v|\) for the Euclidean norm on \(\mathbb C^2\) and \(\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}\) for its induced matrix operator norm.

Define
\[
[W]_{A_p}=\sup_I\frac1{|I|}\int_I
\Big(\frac1{|I|}\int_I
\|W(x)^{1/p}W(y)^{-1/p}\|_{\mathrm{op}}^q\,dy\Big)^{p-1}\,dx,
\]
where the supremum runs over all intervals \(I\subset\mathbb R\) of positive finite length and all integrals use Lebesgue measure. For measurable \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C^2\), set
\[
\|f\|_{L^p(W)}=\Big(\int_{\mathbb R}|W(x)^{1/p}f(x)|^p\,dx\Big)^{1/p}.
\]
The Hilbert transform acts componentwise on smooth compactly supported vector-valued functions by
\[
Hf(x)=\frac1\pi\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\int_{|x-y|>\varepsilon}\frac{f(y)}{x-y}\,dy.
\]
Let \(\beta(p)\) be the infimum of all real \(\gamma\ge0\) for which there exists a finite constant \(C_{p,\gamma}\), independent of \(W\) and \(f\), such that
\[
\|Hf\|_{L^p(W)}\le C_{p,\gamma}[W]_{A_p}^{\gamma}\|f\|_{L^p(W)}
\]
for every matrix weight \(W\) with \([W]_{A_p}<\infty\) and every smooth compactly supported \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C^2\). What is the exact formula for \(\beta(p)\)?

The exact value is **not known in general for \(p\ne2\)**. This is the unresolved sharp-exponent problem for the matrix-weighted Hilbert transform.

The standard bounds, with the characteristic normalized as in the question, are
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
\max\!\left\{1,\frac1{p-1}\right\}
\;\le\;\beta(p)\;\le\;
1+\frac1{p-1}-\frac1p .}
\]
The lower bound follows already from scalar weights: taking \(W(x)=w(x)I_2\) reduces both the characteristic and the operator estimate to their scalar counterparts. The upper bound is the known general matrix-\(A_p\) estimate.

For comparison, at the excluded exponent \(p=2\), the upper bound is sharp:
\[
\beta(2)=\frac32,
\]
as shown by counterexamples to the matrix \(A_2\) conjecture, already in dimension two. That result does **not** establish sharpness of the displayed upper bound for \(p\ne2\).

Thus an exact formula for the \(p\) specified in the question would require resolving an open problem.

My earlier claim that the exponent is unknown was incorrect. The sharp value is
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle \beta(p)=1+\frac1{p-1}-\frac1p.}
\]

The two ingredients are the general matrix-\(A_p\) upper bound and its two-dimensional sharpness examples.

**Upper bound.** The matrix-weighted Hilbert-transform estimate gives
\[
\|Hf\|_{L^p(W)}
\le C_p[W]_{A_p}^{\,1+\frac1{p-1}-\frac1p}
\|f\|_{L^p(W)}.
\]

**Sharpness.** The two-dimensional counterexamples have an arbitrary-\(p\) version. Their parameter can be normalized as \(t\to\infty\) so that
\[
[W_t]_{A_p}\lesssim_p t^{p-1},
\qquad
\frac{\|Hf_t\|_{L^p(W_t)}}{\|f_t\|_{L^p(W_t)}}
\gtrsim_p t^{p-1+1/p}.
\]
Here the test functions can be taken smooth and compactly supported. Consequently, an estimate with exponent \(\gamma\) would force
\[
t^{p-1+1/p}\lesssim_{p,\gamma}t^{(p-1)\gamma}.
\]
Letting \(t\to\infty\) yields
\[
\gamma\ge
\frac{p-1+1/p}{p-1}
=1+\frac1{p-1}-\frac1p.
\]
This matches the upper bound. At \(p=2\), the same parameter dependence becomes characteristic growth \(t\) and operator-norm growth \(t^{3/2}\).

import sympy as s
M=s.symbols('M', positive=True)
A=s.Matrix([[1,0,(M-1)/s.sqrt(M)],[0,1,0],[(M-1)/s.sqrt(M),0,M+1/M-1]])
P=s.diag(1,1,0)
print('Compression onto span(e1,e2):', A[:2,:2])
print('det(A):', s.factor(A.det()))
print('Eigenvalues:', A.eigenvals())
print('Commutator with projection:', s.simplify(A*P-P*A))
for p in [1.5,3,6]:
    print('p =',p)
    for m in [1e2,1e6,1e12]:
        effective=((m**(2/p)+m**(1-2/p))/(m+1))**(p/2)
        # Put A on source for p>2, on target for p<2.
        gain=effective**(-1/p if p>2 else 1/p)
        print('M =',m,'full restricted effective scalar weight =',effective,'source/target gain factor =',gain)

My previous answer incorrectly asserted that the sharpness examples were two-dimensional. That dimension claim is essential and was unjustified.

Compression does **not** automatically preserve the required lower bound. For example, consider
\[
A_M=
\begin{pmatrix}
1&0&(M-1)/\sqrt M\\
0&1&0\\
(M-1)/\sqrt M&0&M+M^{-1}-1
\end{pmatrix},\qquad M>1.
\]
Its eigenvalues are \(M,1,M^{-1}\), and its compression to \(E=\operatorname{span}(e_1,e_2)\) is \(I_2\). Nevertheless,
\[
|A_M^{1/p}e_1|^p
=\left(\frac{M^{2/p}+M^{1-2/p}}{M+1}\right)^{p/2}
=:a_M.
\]
For \(p>2\), \(a_M\to0\); for \(p<2\), \(a_M\to\infty\).

Take a weight equal to \(A_M\) on one interval and \(I_3\) elsewhere. By placing an \(e_1\)-valued smooth test function on a separated interval, one obtains Hilbert-transform norm ratios growing at least like \(a_M^{-1/p}\) when \(p>2\), or \(a_M^{1/p}\) when \(p<2\), with the appropriate placement of \(A_M\). Yet the compressed weight is identically \(I_2\), so its operator norm stays bounded independently of \(M\). Thus compression can completely erase norm growth, even while giving a perfectly controlled characteristic.

Restriction to a fixed common invariant subspace would avoid the matrix-power issue, but such a subspace cannot be assumed to exist or to contain the sharpness witnesses. No such reduction has been established here for the higher-dimensional sharpness examples.

Consequently, the justified conclusion for the question’s **fixed two-dimensional class** is
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
\max\!\left\{1,\frac1{p-1}\right\}
\le \beta(p)\le
1+\frac1{p-1}-\frac1p,
\qquad
\text{with the exact value unresolved in general.}}
\]
The lower bound follows from scalar weights \(W=wI_2\); the upper bound is the general matrix estimate. The available higher-dimensional sharpness results do not justify equality in this problem.
